## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kapotajātaka* (Ja 375) is a story in the *Pañcanipāta* of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1883]. The framing narrative is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha addresses a greedy monk (*lolabhikkhu*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. When the monk acknowledges his greed, the Buddha remarks that not only in the present, but also in a past life, his greed led to his destruction, and he recounts the tale of the past [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. Opening with the words *Idāni khomhi* ("I feel quite well"), the story relates the interactions between a virtuous pigeon (the Bodhisatta) and a greedy crow [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. After admonishing the crow, the pigeon flies away, while the crow meets his death [Fausböll 1883]. Following the exposition of the four noble truths, the monk attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), and the Buddha reveals that the greedy monk had been the crow, while he himself had been the pigeon (*kapoto*) [Fausböll 1883].
In terms of text reuse and parallels, SuttaCentral lists four modern translations across four languages but records no external parallels [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus identifies no cross-language parallels meeting its score threshold [DharmaNexus].
